sections.heading: Recognising accents by sound
sections.body:
- **Seseo** — *s, z* and *ce/ci* all sound like /s/. Standard in all of Latin America and the Canary Islands: *casa* and *caza* sound the same.
- **Distinción** — central/northern Spain pronounces *z, ce, ci* like English "th".
- **Yeísmo** — *ll* and *y* sound the same (nearly everywhere). In the Río de la Plata they sound like "sh" or "zh" (*sheísmo / zheísmo*): *calle* → "cashe".
- **Aspiration of s** — at the end of a syllable, *s* becomes a breathy /h/ or disappears: Caribbean, coastal Colombia and Venezuela, Chile, Argentina, Andalusia: *los amigos* → "loh amigo".
- **Weak final d**: *cansado* → "cansao" (Spain, Caribbean, informal).
- **l/r swap** in the Caribbean: *puerta* → "puelta" (Puerto Rico).
- **Strong, clear consonants and rich vowels** — highland Mexico, Bogotá, Andean Peru and Bolivia.

sections.heading: Current spelling norms (RAE 2010)
sections.body:
- *solo* (only) no longer needs an accent, even when it's an adverb: *Solo quiero agua.* Demonstratives *este, ese, aquel* also go without accent.
- *guion, truhan, fie, lie* (one syllable) — no accent.
- *o* between numbers no longer takes an accent: *3 o 4*.
- *Ex-* is written together with one word: *exnovio, expresidente*; separately with more: *ex primer ministro*.
- Letters: *ye* (not "i griega"), *be* and *uve* (LatAm often *be larga / be corta*).
- Capitals: days, months, languages, nationalities are lowercase: *el lunes, en marzo, el español, los mexicanos*.

sections.heading: Common spelling traps
sections.body: *haber / a ver* (*Va a haber una fiesta.* / *A ver, ¿qué pasa?*), *hay / ahí / ay*, *echo / hecho* (*Te echo de menos. / Lo he hecho.*), *porque / por qué / porqué / por que*, *sino / si no* (*No es rojo, sino azul. / Si no vienes, me enojo.*), *también / tan bien*, *adonde / a donde / adónde*.

examples: En Latinoamérica, casa y caza suenan igual.
In Latin America, casa and caza sound the same.
En Buenos Aires, calle suena como cashe.
In Buenos Aires, calle sounds like 'cashe'.
En el Caribe se aspira la s final.
In the Caribbean the final s is aspirated.
El lunes empiezan las clases de español.
There's going to be a party.
If you don't come, I'll get angry.
—Why didn't you come? —Because I was sick.
Cantas tan bien que también podrías ser profesional.
You sing so well that you could also be a professional.
